title: Arjuna asks: how do I think of you? (10.12–10.18)
hook: Arjuna believes every word, and still asks the most practical question in the book

segments.voice: Yesterday: the source. Your line was I am the origin: everything flows from one spring. Did you and a friend wake each other up a little? Day one hundred ninety-four.

Someone tells you something enormous. The ocean is two miles deep here. The universe is expanding. Your grandmother loved you more than anyone ever will. You believe it. You really do. But then you go and make a sandwich, and you have no idea how to hold that fact while spreading the mustard. Believing a thing and living with it are different skills. Today, Arjuna has just heard that Krishna is the source of everything. He believes it. And then he asks the most practical question in the Gita: okay, but how do I actually think of you?
screen: `SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THEN YOU MAKE A SANDWICH.` → `HOW DO I THINK OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Verse twelve is Arjuna's confession of faith. You are the highest Brahman, the highest home, the highest purifier, the eternal divine person, the first god, unborn, all-pervading. And he adds: all the sages say so. Narada says it, Asita and Devala say it, Vyasa says it. And now you say it yourself. Verse fourteen: I accept everything you've told me as true. Neither the gods nor the demons know your full manifestation. Verse fifteen: only you know yourself, by yourself, highest person, source of beings, god of gods, lord of the world. That's a complete statement of belief. And then, verse seventeen. How shall I know you, master of yoga, by constant meditation? In which things, in which forms, should I think of you? It's a humble question, and a smart one. He's saying: I can't think about everything at once. Give me some handles. Where do I look? Verse sixteen already asked for it: tell me, without leaving anything out, your divine glories, vibhutis, the powers by which you fill all these worlds. And verse eighteen shows how he feels about it. Tell me again, in detail. I never get tired of hearing your words; they're like nectar. So chapter ten isn't a list for its own sake. It's an answer to a person who believes, and wants to know where to put their eyes on an ordinary day. Tomorrow comes the list. Today, the question. That's today's word: Arjuna asks. How to hold it.
screen: `YOU ARE THE HIGHEST BRAHMAN.` · `I ACCEPT IT ALL AS TRUE.` · `IN WHICH THINGS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?` · `TELL ME AGAIN. IT'S NECTAR.` · then, large: `HOW TO HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask Arjuna's question in your own way. Where, in your ordinary day, would it be easiest for you to notice something sacred, or something bigger than you? Maybe first light through a window. A child laughing. The first sip of tea. A piece of music. Let one answer come. Then spend the rest of the sit with it: picture it, feel it, let it be your handle. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna asks. After believing it all, he asks: in which things should I think of you? Give me something to hold.
Your line: how to hold it. Today, take the handle you found and look for it once, on purpose. Day one hundred ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 194 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "I AM THE TASTE IN WATER."`

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep God in mind through particular forms and places: an image at the home shrine, a sacred river, a tree, a name repeated through the day, in the spirit of Arjuna's question in Gita 10.17.

myth: Arjuna doubts what Krishna has said
verse 14: I accept everything you've told me as true.
Arjuna asks for specific things to think of Krishna in
verse 17: in which things, which forms, should I think of you?
verse 18: tell me again, in detail; I never tire of your words.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you believe Krishna is the source of everything. what do you ask next?
options: in which things should I think of you?
fork.reveal: he asks for handles: in which things, which forms, should I think of you? chapter ten's list is the answer.

original.note: Sanskrit: vibhuti, divine glory, manifestation of power; also the sacred ash many Hindus wear.

trapdoor: what you thought: believing is the hard part.
what it means: after believing, Arjuna asks the practical question: where do I look, in which things should I think of you?
what a scholar hears: vibhuti (10.16, 10.18) gives chapter ten its name, vibhuti yoga; the same word also names the sacred ash, especially in Shaiva practice.
